verdicts.note: Faithful: Johnson (Furness) reads the line as the policy being 'satisfied with such slight reasons', i.e. kept alive on very little. 'survive on so thin and watery a diet' says that, and 'so ... a diet' parallels 'so long ... so out of circumstance ... that'. Natural by ear.
The object now comes before the 'into' phrase. Nothing added or lost from 'intermingle everything he does / With Cassio's suit'.
The dash pair voices the parenthesis cleanly. 'offense' is the only other change and is a spelling change. 'not almost a fault' is still correctly rendered 'hardly even'.

'who came along with you when you were courting me' matches 'That came a-wooing with you' (cf. 3.3, where Cassio 'went between us very oft') and removes the Cassio-as-suitor hearing. The when-clause after the verb is natural. 'favor' is a US spelling change.
House style: the only change is 'favour' to 'favor'.
Restores the causal 'For'. Moving 'seeping out from the heart' to the end keeps the noun phrase whole and is easy to follow by ear. Nothing added or lost.

This changes the reading from Johnson's ('no longer ... bear the shape of men') to Jennens's ('have no seeming or appearance of honesty'). Furness gives both, and Jennens's is the plain reading that fits the 'honest' exchange in 9.60-9.63. It is clearer by ear than v1. Record the reading choice under rule 7.

The direction is right: the self-reference must be audible. Two wording problems remain. (a) '— me — Iago,' puts the vocative straight after the appositive, so the ear can take 'me, Iago' as one phrase; putting 'Iago' first removes that. (b) The edit also dropped the image 'mak'st his ear / A stranger to thy thoughts' without giving a reason. Rule 2 says keep the image, and the first-person version keeps it at no cost. 'betraying' is kept as the editor's word.
verdicts.proposed_after: Iago, you're betraying your friend — me — if you even think I've been wronged and keep my ear a stranger to your thoughts.

verdicts.note: 'I beg you — ... — let your wisdom take no notice of me' joins the plea to what is begged. First person replaces Iago's mock-modest third person ('one that so imperfectly conceits ... his scattering and unsure observance'), keeps the content and removes the 'someone else' mishearing.
The relative clause now sits with its noun. The famous 'green-eyed monster, which mocks the meat it feeds on' is unchanged.
The right-dislocation 'he counts out, the man who adores...' is natural spoken English and keeps the order of 'tells he o'er / Who dotes'. The content is complete.
'forming fresh suspicions every time the moon changes' keeps the moon image and attaches the suspicions to Othello, not to the moon.
It now says that the accomplishments become more virtuous, as the original does.
'either love or jealousy' keeps the disjunction (proof ends one or the other) and removes the self-correction effect.

The finite 'she turned down' is a natural way to voice the anacoluthon 'As ... Not to affect many proposed matches'. 'class' for 'degree' is exact and avoids the clash with 'rank' in the next unit. The closing dash leads cleanly into 'ugh!'.
The merge is right, and 'that' after 'fear' prevents the garden path. 'returns to' for 'recoiling to' and 'perhaps regret her choice' for 'happily repent' are faithful.
'your lordship' is the right modern courtesy for a nobleman. 'Your Honor' now suggests a judge.
Same as E17.
The merge is right, and the noun phrase is closed up. 'every type of human behavior' fits Schmidt, who files this line under quality 2 ('nature, character').

Unstacking the compound is right, but the new wording narrows and skews the line. Schmidt glosses 'conversation' at this very line as 'address, deportment' (sense 3), so 'talk' is too narrow. 'who frequent bedrooms' sounds odd by ear and pushes 'chamberers' further toward the bedroom than the original does. Onions gives 'frequenter of ladies' chambers, gallant'; Schmidt gives 'a man conversant with the arts of peace, opposed to a soldier'; Steevens gives 'men of intrigue'. 'manners' and 'women's chambers' keep both the social-graces sense and the wanton sense.
verdicts.proposed_after: and don't have the smooth, charming manners of the ladies' men who frequent women's chambers, or because I've gone down

verdicts.note: The sense is correct: great men are less privileged against it than the base (see Malone in Furness). The line now connects to the plague of cuckoldry.

The gloss is not invented. Percy (Furness) reads 'forked plague' as 'the horns of the cuckold', and Rymer and Delius read the forehead pain at 9.105 as this allusion. It is a short appositive, not a footnote. The problem is new: 'even then' now opens the clause straight after 'like death:', so the listener hears 'even at death'. Modern English has no 'then ... when' correlative to resolve it forward, and 'from the moment we're conceived' comes too late. Attach 'even' to the conception phrase instead. This keeps the restored emphasis.
verdicts.proposed_after: this forked plague — horns growing from a betrayed husband's forehead — is fated for us even from the moment we're conceived. Here comes Desdemona.

verdicts.note: Naming the Moor removes the Iago mishearing, and Emilia uses 'the Moor' two lines earlier. Separately, the v1 wording 'made her swear' slightly strengthens 'conjur'd her', which Schmidt (conjure 2) glosses 'to call on with solemnity'. 'solemnly charged her to keep it always' would be exact. This is optional.
'here' breaks the modern romantic idiom and keeps 'thing' free for Iago's pun.

'Your thing's a common thing' makes the bawdy sense (thing = her sex, common = shared by all) audible at the original's strength without adding obscenity. 9.118 supplies the innocent sense, so both senses reach the ear, as rule 4 requires.
'What?' is neutral and safe for the period; 'Huh?' was too casual.
Restating 'it's common' after the interruption lets the listener hear Iago swerve to the proverb-like insult. The leading spaced dash marks the continuation.

Restating the subject fixes 'the blood burn', but it creates a punctuation fault. The new colon after 'poisons' follows the colon that already ends line 4 ('changing under my poison:'), so v2 now has two colons in one sentence. Use a semicolon.
verdicts.proposed_after: dangerous suspicions are by nature poisons; at first they barely taste unpleasant, but once they start working a little on the blood, they burn like sulfur mines. Just as I said.

verdicts.note: 'Oh! Oh!' voices a cry of shock; TTS would read 'Ha! Ha!' as laughter.
Natural. 'sense' means awareness (Schmidt sense 3).

Schmidt files 'all q., pride, pomp and circumstance of glorious war' under quality 2 ('nature, character'), and Onions gives that as the commonest sense. 'all the qualities' removes the invented 'rank' and 'splendor'. It is slightly abstract by ear, but the list after it explains it.
The line is famous and already clear (occupation = profession). Rule 2 applies.
'Goodbye' is what 'God be wi' you' means here. Turning the self-apostrophe into 'what a wretched fool I am' keeps the content and stops it being heard as aimed at Othello.
Keeps 'satisfied' for Iago's echoes in 9.150-9.152 ('You want to be satisfied?', 'How satisfied, my lord?'). The short appositive sounds like speech, not like a footnote.
'get them where you could see them like that' is the sense of 'bring them to that prospect'. 'any mortal eyes but their own' puts the exception next to its noun.
'prime' means lustful (Onions). 'lecherous' is as strong without modern slang, and it varies with 'hot' and 'lustful' after it.
The order is natural. The aside becomes a trailing dash clause, and 'it' clearly means the handkerchief.
'slave' as abuse means villain or wretch. 'scoundrel' keeps the contempt and avoids a literal hearing, which is loaded in this play.
'load' keeps 'fraught' (freight, burden) and reads naturally. 'heart' for 'bosom' echoes 'the throne in my heart', but it is heard as the same heart now filled with venom, which fits the image.
Restores the original word. With 'lewd', the insult is clear, and it avoids the US/UK split in the meaning of 'tramp'.
'You there' is the right register for a lady's 'sirrah' to a servant.

'fruitfulness' is the original word and is current. It keeps both fertility and bounty open: Schmidt glosses it 'liberality', and Furness records the old opinion that a moist palm indicates a hot liver. The added 'body' is gone.
'free' carries both of Schmidt's senses of 'frank' (unrestrained; liberal), and it lets Desdemona's innocent reply in 10.27 work. 'an easy one' had spelled out the slur.
'I fear the worst' means 'My mind misgives' and avoids the film catchphrase.
A modern plea construction. The content is complete ('Exist' = come back to life; 'be a member of his love' = have a place in his love).
The 'blank' is the white centre of the target. 'bull's-eye' is the idiomatic modern word and keeps the archery image.
Natural and faithful to 'went hence but now ... in strange unquietness'.
Schmidt (ever 2): 'not e. = not always'. Keeps Emilia's qualification, and the scope of 'not always' reads correctly by ear.
House style: the only change is 'honour' to 'honor'.
House style: the only change is 'honour' to 'honor'.
The merge is right. The respective pairing is kept in modern order: importunate suit goes with 'won over', and a mistress's voluntary dotage goes with 'satisfied'.
Removes an added oath. 'fulsome' is still rendered as 'disgusting'.
Onions gives both senses ('made my reckoning' and 'branded me'), and the line now carries both. It avoids 'scored', now sexual slang, and 'marked me down', which now suggests a price cut.
'she shall not live' keeps Othello's resolve; 'won't live' was heard as a prediction.
Natural order; the content is unchanged.
Rule 7 applies: Iago's riddle stays open, and Lodovico's question just before (11.161, 'unhinged') already supplies the madness hint.
House style: the only change is 'behaviour' to 'behavior'.
'a cupboard kept under lock and key, full of vile secrets' parses by ear and keeps the image of 'A closet lock and key'.
Matches Johnson in Furness ('thyself change colour'). It keeps 'complexion' and does not choose a direction of colour.
'Is hush'd' means falls silent; the stillness image is restored.
Punctuation only. The commas mark the appositive, so the conditional subject is heard as one unit.
Rolfe in Furness glosses it 'it fills me with horror' and calls it the only instance of this sense. 'abhorrence' keeps both the exact sense and the abhor/whore sound.
Schmidt lists IV.2.203 under both 'payment' and 'amends, atonement'. 'demand satisfaction' alone keeps that openness, and the invented duel is gone.
'do yourself ... a right' means do yourself justice. 'get yourself justice' is close and removes the added entitlement.
The merge is right. 'I love him so much that' stops 'my love' being heard as a person, and the stray article is gone ('grace and charm').
'it does' now points back to 'does that mean I'm going to cry?' (13.33), not to Emilia's dismissal in 13.34.
'an appetite for sexual sport' removes the 'desires, a desire' stutter and is faithful to 'Desires for sport'.
Keeps it a moral question, with its irony in Iago's mouth.

The revert is confirmed. Furness records Johnson, Steevens, Hudson and White on 'the cause': it is the motive, the provocation, or a cause maintained, and White calls it perplexing. None gives a courtroom frame, and Schmidt (cause 1) gives 'motive'. Modern 'the cause' keeps all these readings open and does not half-name what Othello refuses to name (rule 7). It also restores the famous incantatory repetition (rule 2).

'I won't name it' renders Othello's self-restraint ('Let me not name it'), not a plea to the stars. Separately, the v1 wording 'pure, chaste' doubles 'chaste'; 'you chaste stars' alone would be exact. This is optional.

'monumental alabaster' means the alabaster of tomb effigies, so 'a statue on a tomb' is right and keeps the death image. Line 2 is confirmed: 'It's the cause. Still, I won't spill her blood,' keeps the third refrain unglossed (G1 agrees), renders 'Yet' (nevertheless) as 'Still,' and renders 'shed' as 'spill'. It is faithful and clear. Optionally, 'Yet I won't shed her blood' would sit closer to the famous wording.
'roll wildly' keeps the rolling eyes and signals rage rather than modern eye-rolling.
'the ordinary love that heaven allows me to feel for anyone' means 'such general warranty of heaven / As I might love', and the 'heaven allows that...' misparse is gone.
'has had you' is as veiled as 'us'd', and it leaves Desdemona's 'Unlawfully?' (15.39) logical.
Correct modern past counterfactual.
'Are you there?' fits someone calling through a locked door, where 'Hello there!' sounded like a greeting.

'So, so' goes with the renewed smothering: Delius reads it as Othello stifling her again, and Cowden Clarke as pressing the pillow closer (both in Furness). 'Like this. Like this.' voices the action and avoids the comforting 'There, there'. It matches 'like this' for 'thus' at 15.190.
Same as E76.
Not invented: Othello names Emilia at the start of this same speech. The name separates the two 'she's (Desdemona dead, Emilia at the door) and sounds like speech, not like a footnote.
Restores 'chrysolite' with a one-word gloss. 'another world like this one' means 'such another world'. 'Listen —' voices 'Nay' as an intensifier, not as a negation.
The comparison now parses by ear: her capacity to endure is more than twice his power to hurt.
'a fine job, if' makes the sarcasm audible.
The charm image is now part of the imperative, with no appended gloss.
The dash and the resumptive 'it' keep the emphatic fronting without a garden path.
'a wife as good as yours' makes clear that Emilia means Desdemona.
'taken from the Moor' means 'recover'd from the Moor' (got from him) and no longer implies the sword was Montano's.
Not invented: 'him' is Othello, and 'that same villain' is Iago, whom Montano has just called a notorious villain. Naming them fixes the pronoun flip and sounds like speech, not annotation.

The revert is confirmed. Both words are current and the line is clear (rule 2). Walker (in Furness) notes that each word could carry both meanings, so 'my reputation ... my integrity' narrowed them and decided whose honesty is meant. The revert also keeps the honest/honesty chain.
The plain oath formula keeps the stake.

The stated basis is wrong. Schmidt (naked 3) and Onions (naked 2) both gloss this very line as 'unarmed', and White in Furness reads it as 'weaponless, as Gratiano supposes him'. The contradiction with the sword Othello has just found is the point. He echoes Gratiano's 'You have no weapon' (15.157) to lure him in, then says 'Look, I have a weapon' (15.161). 'defenseless' has no lexicon support, blurs the echo, and does not remove the contradiction the blind reader heard. Do not add 'as you think': that would give away the bluff to Gratiano. Restore BEFORE: 'or, unarmed as I am, I'll attack you.'
The contortion is gone, and 'I cut my way' fixes the tense mix. 'twenty times what you put in my way' means 'twenty times your stop', and 'what an empty boast' means 'O vain boast'.
The short gloss unpacks Othello's approval of Iago's vow of silence (15.177) and stops it being heard as approving torture.
Schmidt (base 3) gives 'mean, vile'. 'ignorant' belonged to the Q 'Indian' reading, not to F1 'Judean'. 'base' itself is still current and would keep the famous wording. This is optional.

Clearer than v1. Schmidt glosses 'all that's spoke is marred' as 'has been spoken in vain'. After Lodovico's 'bloody period' (full stop), 'he said' is a fair reading. Optionally, 'everything that's been said' would keep Schmidt's wider scope.

The dashes attach 'because he had a great heart' to 'I was afraid of this', as the original intends. 'great of heart' means high-spirited and magnanimous (Schmidt, great 5), and the plain wording keeps that open.
Modern order, and the 'heavy ... heavy' echo is kept.

summary: RC2 re-checked all 96 edits in chapters 9-15 against pg1531, Schmidt, Onions and Furness: 91 accept, 4 revise (E8 9.67, E20 9.100, E22 9.100, E28 9.130), 1 reject (E90 15.158). Attention items: the 15.2 line-0 revert is accepted, and line 2 ('It's the cause. Still, I won't spill her blood,') is confirmed as faithful. The 15.153 revert is accepted. None of the listener glosses is invented: 9.100's horns (Percy, Rymer and Delius in Furness), the names at 15.61 and 15.151, 'keeping quiet' at 15.180, and 'satisfied — that I knew for certain' at 9.149. 9.100 needs a fix only because the restored 'even then' is now heard as 'even at death'. E90 rests on a misreading of Schmidt: Schmidt and Onions both gloss 'naked' at this line as 'unarmed', and White reads it as weaponless, as Gratiano supposes. The house-style edits E5, E49, E50 and E57 change spelling only. No AFTER text breaks the conventions, and every AFTER string is present in v2. All 22 re-cut Compare paragraphs tile both texts contiguously, and no modern span carries content from outside its original span. Items 1.33, 3.24 and 3.33 are outside this packet.
